bp.wheel.aria: The chip innovation ecosystem as one wheel: a chip's life around it, from Open to Use, and its scale inward, from the world to the atom.
bp.actor.buyers.d: Cloud companies and the makers of phones and cars decide what gets built. The world bought $795.6 billion of chips in 2025.
bp.actor.community.d: Learners, hobbyists and researchers who share designs, tools and questions in the open.
bp.actor.designers.d: Designing one leading chip at 2 nm costs about $725 million, so only a few can afford to start.
bp.actor.eda.d: Three companies make most chip-design software, and all three now ship AI agents that run it.
bp.actor.riscv.d: An open instruction set anyone can build on without a licence; whole computers now run Linux on it.
bp.actor.openflow.d: Free software turns a description into a chip: Yosys makes the gates, OpenROAD places and wires them.
bp.actor.foundry.d: One leading factory module costs about $25–35 billion and makes about 20,000 wafers a month.
bp.actor.scanner.d: The newest machines that print the finest lines cost about $400 million each, and one company makes them.
bp.actor.pdk.d: Since 2020 the rules of real factory processes have been published openly, so anyone can design for them.
bp.actor.shuttle.d: Many designs share one wafer: about $7,000 buys 1,000 finished chips on an open process.
bp.actor.packaging.d: AI chips need advanced packaging that puts memory beside the logic; one company holds about 70% of it in 2026.
bp.actor.tinytapeout.d: A shared chip where anyone's small design, about 1,000 cells, is made alongside hundreds of others.
bp.actor.devices.d: 1.15 trillion chips were shipped in 2021: about 145 for every person on Earth.
bp.actor.cars.d: A car held about 820 chips in 2022, heading for about 1,100 by 2027.
bp.actor.boards.d: A 32-bit RISC-V microcontroller now costs less than 10 cents.
bp.actor.cloud.d: They used about 485 TWh of electricity, heading for about 950 TWh by 2030.
bp.actor.everyone.d: Computing and communications use 57% of chips; then cars, factories and homes.
bp.wall.switch.d: At room temperature an ordinary switch needs about 60 millivolts more on its gate to let ten times more current through. That is why chip voltages stopped falling, and why every switch still leaks.
bp.wall.memory.d: Reading 16 bits from memory costs about 3,500 times the energy of adding two 16-bit numbers. Most of a computer's energy goes on moving numbers, not on computing with them.
bp.wall.power.d: Data centres used about 485 TWh of electricity and are heading for about 950 TWh by 2030. Each answer gets cheaper, and the world asks for far more of them.
bp.wall.cost.d: A leading factory module costs about $25–35 billion, and designing one leading chip about $725 million. Fewer and fewer can afford the next step.
bp.next.switches.d: Switches that tunnel, sheets one atom thick, carbon nanotubes: ways to turn on more sharply than the 60 mV wall allows, or to stay sharp when tiny.
bp.next.living.d: Human neurons grown on a silicon chip, sold as a computer since 2025 for about $35,000. A brain thinks on about 20 W.
bp.next.cim.d: Do the sums where the numbers are stored, with currents adding up on a wire; one analog chip claims about 20 times the work per watt.
bp.next.stack.d: Stacks of memory beside the logic in one package, so numbers travel millimetres, not centimetres; the newest kind went into mass production in 2026.
bp.next.light.d: Optics packaged with the switch chips themselves, so data crosses a data centre as light; in production since 2026.
bp.next.spikes.d: Neurons that fire only when something changes: one research system joins 1,152 chips into 1.15 billion neurons.
bp.next.pbits.d: Let heat's randomness do the computing, or never erase a bit at all; erasing one has been measured to release heat close to the physical floor.
bp.next.liquid.d: Circuits that can be rewired after they are made, from today's FPGAs to fabrics rewired every tick.
bp.next.machines.d: No standard computer at all: a machine put together for one need from shared blocks, by people and AI together.
bp.next.smallfab.d: No cleanroom and half-inch wafers, at a hundredth to a thousandth of the cost, for small runs.
bp.lang.note: Only this first page is translated so far; the rest of the lab is in English.
bp.hero.k: Open Silicon Lab · a blueprint for what comes next
bp.hero.p: Every chip ever made has gone round one loop, from something open to something used, and has been built from the world down to the atom. Here is all of it on one sheet: who makes chips, the walls they have hit, what is being tried next, and how people and AI will build the next machine together.
bp.stages.aria: The six stages of a chip's life
bp.ch.whole.h: One loop around, every scale inward
bp.ch.whole.p: Around the wheel runs a chip's life: something open (a need, or a thing that has just become possible), then designed, made, tested, shipped and used; and what its users learn opens the next. Inward runs its scale, from the whole world at the rim to a single atom at the centre. Three lines cross it: design comes down from a need to the masks, the factory builds back up from a crystal, and the dive goes straight down through a chip at work.
bp.ch.world.h: A trillion chips a year, made by a handful and used by everyone
bp.ch.world.p: Around the rim stand the people and companies who make chips happen. At the giant end, one leading factory costs tens of billions of dollars and a single company builds the machines that print the finest lines. At the open end, anyone can now design a chip with free tools and an open instruction set, and have a thousand made for about $7,000.
bp.ch.walls.h: Four walls the next machine has to get past
bp.ch.walls.p: For fifty years chips got smaller, faster and cheaper all at once. That ride has slowed against walls that are physical, not only hard: a switch that cannot turn on any sharper at room temperature, numbers that cost more to move than to compute with, data centres that need power stations of their own, and factories so costly that only a few can build them.
bp.ch.next.h: Ten ways people are trying to get past the walls
bp.ch.next.p: Some are in products you can buy today, some have only been shown in a lab, and some are still a guess. Each sits on the wheel where it works, with a line to the wall it attacks. None of them is the answer yet: the next architecture is still open.
bp.ch.people.h: Who generates, who checks, who decides
bp.ch.people.p: AI is already inside the tools that design, make and test chips. As it generates more of the work, the question is not whether people stay in the loop but where: deciding what a chip is for, choosing what to give up, judging what an AI made, and breaking it before the world does. In the middle of the wheel is the loop this lab itself runs on.
bp.ch.you.h: The next machine is open. So is this lab.
bp.ch.you.p: Every glowing place on the wheel is open work, read from the lab's record: a design nobody has broken, a piece nobody has built, a question nobody has answered. Anyone can take one, and so can any AI agent through the lab's open port. Nobody votes and nobody gives points: what stands is what survives the checks.
bp.ch.whole.hint: Every dot is a place in the lab: tap one to go there, or pick a stage to see what lives in it.
bp.ch.world.hint: Switch between the two ends, and tap anyone on the rim to see what they do.
bp.ai.label: How much of the work AI generates
bp.ai.note0: Today: what is already true, from the sources.
bp.ai.note1: A question, not a forecast: if AI generated more, which decisions would still be people's?
bp.ai.note2: A question, not a forecast: even when AI generates most of the work, a share stays with people, and it is the share that matters most.
bp.role.open.ai: finds patterns in papers, data and needs, and proposes what might be possible
bp.role.open.people: decide which needs matter, and for whom
bp.role.design.ai: writes and checks designs, places the cells and draws the wires; agents now run the design tools
bp.role.design.people: choose the trade-offs, set the rules, and judge what the agent made
bp.role.make.ai: tunes the printing, spots defects, and runs a digital twin of the factory
bp.role.make.people: decide what to make, where, and with what; and the industry is short of people to do it
bp.role.test.ai: generates the tests and checks the designs, up to 50 times faster by one tool maker's claim
bp.role.test.people: decide when it is good enough, and sign their names to it
bp.role.ship.ai: plans the supply and forecasts the demand
bp.role.ship.people: decide who gets chips first when there are not enough
bp.role.use.ai: runs on the chips, and asks for more of them
bp.role.use.people: ask the questions worth the energy
bp.you.people: added by a person so far
bp.door.invent.d: A machine of shared blocks for one need, or a switch of your own against silicon.
bp.door.build.d: A piece of the shared open computer, checked by the lab's engines.
bp.door.break.d: Find the case that makes a design wrong: a break is the most useful thing anyone can add.
bp.door.ask.d: Questions with no answer yet, each one a way deeper.
bp.stage.open.d: Where the loop starts and comes back: something someone needs, or something that has just become possible.
bp.stage.design.d: From a need to the masks: what the chip should do, its architecture, its description, its checks, gates and layout.
bp.stage.make.d: From a crystal to a finished wafer: printing, etching and building up, layer after layer.
bp.stage.test.d: Every chip on the wafer tested, the bad ones marked, the good ones packaged.
bp.stage.ship.d: Into phones, cars and servers, and out into the world.
bp.stage.use.d: Where chips do their work: from a data centre down through a chip to its atoms.
bp.card.question: The question behind it
